definition: Instantaneously trained neural networks are feedforward artificial neural networks that create a new hidden neuron node for each novel training sample.
details: The weights to this hidden neuron separate out not only this training sample but others that are near it, thus providing generalization. This separation is done using the nearest hyperplane that can be written down instantaneously. In the two most important implementations the neighborhood of generalization either varies with the training sample (CC1 network) or remains constant (CC4 network). These networks use unary coding for an effective representation of the data sets. This type of network was first proposed in a 1993 paper of Subhash Kak. Since then, instantaneously trained neural networks have been proposed as models of short term learning and used in web search, and financial time series prediction applications. They have also been used in instant classification of documents and for deep learning and data mining. As in other neural networks, their normal use is as software, but they have also been implemented in hardware using FPGAs and by optical implementation.

explainer.lead: Feedforward networks that create a new hidden neuron for each novel training sample, with weights that separate that sample and its neighbours. It matters because this gives generalization while training in one pass.

tiers.eli5: Like adding a new labelled drawer for each new item, placed so nearby similar items end up together.
tiers.practitioner: Engineers add a hidden neuron per new sample, using the nearest writable hyperplane so nearby samples are also captured. A pitfall is choosing between varying neighbourhoods (CC1) and constant ones (CC4).
tiers.paperLevel: Feedforward networks adding one hidden neuron per novel sample, weights separating it and nearby samples via the nearest hyperplane written down instantaneously; neighbourhood varies in CC1 and is constant in CC4, using unary coding.

explainer.example: A new training sample triggers a hidden neuron whose weights also separate nearby samples, giving generalization without iterative training.
